description: Every class and method of the scripting API, a line each (also: redgem api).
about: The scripting API of RedGem games: the classes and methods scripts use. Generated from docs/scripting/api.json, which tests keep in step with the engine.
notes: Script errors are logged with a backtrace and only disable the failing behaviour; the game keeps running. Every method takes finite numbers a float can hold: infinity, NaN or a number too large raises an `ArgumentError` instead of reaching the scene. A setting with a range raises outside it and says the range; nothing is quietly clamped, except `Vehicle#drive`'s inputs. Assigning `transform.position` to a physics object teleports it (moving bodies also stop); changing its rotation keeps its velocity. Images may be PNG, JPEG or static WebP (a name without an extension looks for `.webp`, then `.ktx2`, last), at most 8192 pixels a side; animated WebP is not read. Images may also be KTX2 (Basis Universal): decoded to RGBA8, except a scene's textures (glTF's `KHR_texture_basisu`), kept compressed on the graphics card. Missing or unreadable images (scene textures, `UI.image`, particle images) show an opaque magenta-and-black checkerboard, with a warning; a material that never named a texture keeps its plain color, and no path reads outside the game's folder.

classes.notes: `==` compares the numbers exactly, and equal vectors are one key of a `Hash`. A vector used as a key must not be changed in place (`set`, `add!`...) while the `Hash` holds it: use a `dup` as the key. The scene keeps positions, rotations and scales in 32-bit floats, so a vector that goes through it comes back rounded: compare what comes back from the scene with `approx?(other, tolerance)`. The in-place methods change the vector and hand it back: `dup` one you got from someone else first. Arithmetic whose result would not fit a float, and dividing by zero, raise an `ArgumentError`; a vector changed in place is then left as it was.

classes.name: Navigation
classes.about: Where the characters a game moves can walk, and the way from one place to another.

methods.name: path
methods.about: the points to walk through from near `from` to near `to` (Vector3s, both ends included), or nil when there is no way there; `avoid:` game objects whose bodies it keeps a character's width off

methods.name: steer
methods.about: the flat velocity nearest `preferred` that keeps clear of `crowd` ([position, velocity, radius] each, characters that steer too) and of the bodies that move near `position` (but `ignore`), and on walkable ground
methods.example: velocity = Navigation.steer(transform.position, velocity, toward * 3.0, speed: 3.0, radius: 0.4, ignore: game_object)

methods.name: nearest
methods.about: the walkable point nearest a point (within 8 m of it), or nil

methods.name: walkable?
methods.about: whether a point is on walkable ground, up to a character's height above it

methods.name: draw
methods.about: shows the walkable cells within a radius for this frame, as Debug.box does; returns how many

methods.name: bake
methods.about: bakes the scene's grid again now (a level a script changed); returns what stats does

methods.name: stats
methods.about: how the grid was baked: {columns:, cells:, cell_size:, cells_enlarged:, milliseconds:}

classes.notes: The grid is baked from the scene's static bodies as it loads when game.json has a `navigation` section (`cell_size` 0.25, `agent_radius` 0.4, `agent_height` 1.8, `max_step` 0.4, `max_slope` 45 degrees, `bake_on_load` true), and otherwise when a script first asks. Moving bodies, characters and triggers are not in the grid: a path goes around those of `avoid:`, and `steer` (or a NavAgent) around the rest, looking 3 seconds ahead. A level changed after the bake is not seen until `Navigation.bake`. A path goes through cells side by side no more than `max_step` apart, never cutting a corner, and is pulled straight. A search looks at no more than 16384 cells: a way longer than that gives nil, as one to a place nobody can reach does. A grid has at most 262144 columns: a larger level is baked with larger cells, with a warning.

classes.name: Water

methods.name: height_at
methods.about: the height of the water surface over that point of the ground, or nil where there is no water

methods.name: depth_at
methods.about: how far below the water surface a point is in meters (negative above it), or nil where there is no water

methods.name: under?
methods.about: whether a point is below the water surface

classes.notes: Every surface whose material has `water = true` fills the column under it down to whatever ground the level has, or to the next surface below. `height_at` gives the highest surface over a column; `depth_at` and `under?` look at the nearest surface above the point (or, with none above, the nearest below), so a point under a pool on a roof is in the lake beneath it. Heights are the calm surface: waves are not counted. The answers follow the water as the last physics step found it, and are nil (or false) outside a running game.

classes.notes: Every sound played gets an id, flat (`play`) or positional (`play_at`) alike: `stop`, `playing?` and `set` take either. A sound that does not loop is decoded once and each play is a voice of its own; loops and music stream, so a crossfade plays two tracks for its length. A sound plays in a mix group, `:music`, `:effects` (the default) or `:voice`, and is heard at its volume times the player's volume of its group (`Settings.music_volume`, `effects_volume`, `voice_volume`) times the master volume. A game makes groups of its own with `Audio.group(:cave, parent: :effects, volume: 0.8)`, 13 at most, and plays sounds in them by name; a group is heard at its volume times the volumes of the groups over it, and the game's groups end with it. `Audio.effects(group, low_pass:, reverb:)` puts effects on the sounds of a group and of the groups under it: `low_pass` (20 to 20000 Hz) muffles them, and the lowest cutoff over a sound is the one it gets; `reverb` (0 to 1) sends that much of each sound to the reverb of the nearest group that has one. Effects are on sounds, not on the music's tracks. A track that cannot play leaves the one playing as it was. While a sound of the `:voice` group plays, the music and the sounds of the `:music` group duck: they go down to `volume` (0.4 unless `Audio.ducking` says) over `attack` seconds, and come back over `release` seconds once no voice plays. `play_at` sources use stereo panning and inverse-distance volume, fading to silence at `max_distance`. Every frame a ray from the listener to each `play_at` sound in reach looks for the level's static bodies (walls, floors; moving bodies and characters do not count): a sound behind one fades, over `fade` seconds, to `Audio.occlusion`'s `volume` and through its `low_pass`; `occlusion: false` on `play_at` keeps a sound out of it. `volume` must be 0 or more and `pitch` from 0.01 to 8; `0 < reference_distance < max_distance`. Positions and directions may be arrays or `Vector3`. Update `Audio.listener(position, forward, up)` when the camera moves: nothing follows an object by itself. At most 128 sounds with ids play at once. Past that, a new sound takes the place of the weakest one playing (the lowest `priority`, a whole number from 0 to 255, then the quietest as heard, then the oldest) when its priority is at least that one's: that one stops. Otherwise it does not play and gets `nil`. Old ids are never reused.

classes.notes: A focused widget (`focused: true`) is worked by Enter or a gamepad's A, and left and right change it. An anchor (`:top_left`, `:top`, `:top_right`, `:left`, `:center`, `:right`, `:bottom_left`, `:bottom`, `:bottom_right`) makes x and y offsets from that point of the screen, and puts the matching corner of what is drawn there: `UI.text("Lives", anchor: :top_right, x: -20, y: 20)`. With an anchor, a text's box is as wide as `width:` or its widest line, and `align:` lays its lines out inside it; an image is placed by the width and height given. A text breaks at its own line breaks, and with `width:` also at spaces; a word longer than a line is cut between letters. Lines are `UI.line_height(size)` apart (1.25 times the size). Inside `UI.clip`, the pointer outside the box is over nothing drawn in it. The built-in face adds glyphs as they are asked for (Greek, Cyrillic, accented letters, `€`); for another face or script, put a `.ttf` or `.otf` in `fonts/` and set `UI.font`. For several scripts, set a fallback chain: `UI.font = [:latin, :cjk, :emoji]`. A missing or unreadable face falls back to the built-in one, with a warning; glyphs no face has show as the built-in face's `?`. Right-to-left text (Arabic, Hebrew) is drawn in its order on screen, line by line, with its brackets mirrored; Arabic letters are not joined (there is no shaping), and only outline (not color) emoji faces are drawn.

classes.notes: Profiling is off by default. The overlay uses the shared game HUD, including editor Play and recordings; it is hidden when profiling is off. Timings use the real steady clock, independently of Time.scale or fixed-step replay. The most recent 120 completed frames form the window; reads during a frame expose only completed frames. FPS uses completion-to-completion intervals, and is zero until an interval is available. `latest`, `mean` and `peak` contain `frame_ms`, `interval_ms`, `has_interval`, and `input_ms`, `network_ms`, `http_ms`, `update_ms`, `physics_ms`, `presentation_ms`, `scene_ms`. Input includes pending script startup; network and HTTP include their callbacks; update includes animations, scripts, particles, loading UI and physics. Physics includes fixed-update callbacks, body synchronization and contacts, so its time overlaps update. Presentation includes uploads, drawing and any frame-cap or synchronization waits. Scene includes request polling, synchronous reads and activation; the asynchronous worker is not instrumented, while offline fixed-step waits count as scene wall time. These are foreground wall times, not CPU utilization. Where the graphics card can time its work (desktop OpenGL 3.3), the overlay also shows its time over the prepare, scene and post passes, read a frame or more late so the game never waits for the card; it shows none on OpenGL ES. While profiling, a sampling profiler reads the scripts' call stack about every millisecond of Ruby running and the overlay lists the five methods with the most self samples; time in the engine's own functions counts for the Ruby method that called them. Phase times are inclusive and must not be summed as a partition. Overlay timings and captures are nondeterministic; leave the overlay off for reproducible pictures. Debug.line and Debug.box use world coordinates and live for one frame: submit from ready/update/fixed_update. At most 4096 commands are accepted per frame; later calls return false. They are local-only and return false without a presenter, while still validating arguments. depth_test: false draws through objects. Shape frames use unjittered rendering and reset temporal history; normal temporal sampling resumes afterwards. Native windows allocate one cached color/depth target only when shapes are requested; editor, scaled and recorded views reuse their target. If that extra native target is unavailable, the game still draws with a warning and the shapes are omitted. Debug.label places its text after the frame's scripts, as the main camera then sees the point, over the game's interface and under the overlay; at most 256 labels a frame, of at most 256 bytes and a size of 1 to 256 pixels. Nothing is shown for a point behind the camera or without a main camera.

classes.notes:
While an asynchronous read is pending, physics, animations and normal behaviour callbacks pause.
Input, networking, HTTP callbacks, audio and presentation continue. The loading callback can use
`UI`, handle cancel buttons and animate using its unscaled delta; `Time.delta` is zero during
loading. The pointer is released while the screen is shown. The default screen draws a translated
loading label over the old world. A callback error is reported once and disables it for that load.

Unsafe names are rejected immediately; missing or unreadable files are reported through
`Game.loading_error` after the request runs. The old world stays intact if reading fails or is cancelled. The most recent request wins;
`Game.load_scene` also supersedes an asynchronous request. Globals survive successful activation,
but the old scene's loading callback is removed before the next scene's setup runs. Errors are
reported through `Game.loading_error` and the event log. At most eight background requests/results can be
outstanding across the process, using one shared reader; a full queue fails without changing the
world. Cancelling an active read discards its result; it does not interrupt the file parser.

File reading, glTF parsing and, for a game shown in a window, picture decoding happen on the
worker. The scene read is then made ready over the next loading frames while the old one is still
shown: its physics bodies are made in batches of about 4 ms a frame, its textures and meshes go to
the graphics card about 8 MiB a frame, and the swap happens once all of it is ready. Every script
of the new scene starts in that one frame, so a behaviour's first update sees the complete level.
Creating the scene's objects, its water and its navigation bake still take one frame each. The old
and incoming scene coexist in memory until the swap. Fixed-step offline runs (including
recordings and scripted replays) wait for the reader before advancing, then make the scene ready
all at once after exactly one loading frame, so completion depends neither on thread scheduling
nor on the real clock. Networked runs and dedicated-server rooms keep the background reader and
the spread activation even in fixed-step mode; a dedicated server's rooms share their loop. Closing the process waits for an active parser to return.

classes.notes: Values are numbers, texts, true/false, `Vector3`, and arrays and hashes of those; hashes come back with string keys. Named slots start on default for every engine and keep their selection across scenes. Selection is local to each engine, including shared-database server rooms. Names are 1–48 lowercase ASCII letters/digits, hyphens or underscores, starting with a letter/digit. At most 64 named stores may be opened per run/local backend and 4096 names listed; invalid names or unavailable backends leave selection unchanged and raise a Ruby error. The existing default file/table is preserved. Named files use their own atomic writes/backups; SQLite uses separate slot tables. Save.update writes to its entry store even if its block selects another slot. Each slot records the Save.version that wrote it: the first use of a slot (or Save.slot =) runs the migration hooks it needs, in order, and writes the result back at once; a slot from a newer game, or one a hook raised on, is left untouched and every use of it raises a RuntimeError saying why (Save.slot = then keeps the previous slot). A slot written before the game declared a version counts as version 1.
